intro: AQA Higher style. You may use a calculator. Show your working for calculations and write full sentences for the longer answers.

questions.q: Which unit is used for pressure?
questions.ms: Pa (pascal), which is the same as N/m².

questions.q:
A cyclist travels 4.5 km in 15 minutes.
Calculate the cyclist's average speed in m/s.
questions.ms: 5 m/s. M1 4.5 km = 4500 m and 15 min = 900 s, M1 speed = distance ÷ time, A1 4500 ÷ 900 = 5.

questions.q: Explain the difference between average speed and instantaneous speed.
questions.ms: Average speed is total distance ÷ total time for the whole journey (1). Instantaneous speed is the speed at one particular moment, e.g. shown on a speedometer (1).

questions.q:
Car A travels at 70 km/h. Car B travels at 55 km/h in the same direction.
What is the speed of car A relative to car B, in km/h?
The two cars now drive towards each other at the same speeds. Explain why their relative speed is 125 km/h.
questions.ms: Moving in opposite directions, so the speeds add (1): 70 + 55 = 125 km/h (1).

questions.q: Use the graph to calculate the speed in section C.
Is the runner faster in section A or section C? Use the graph to explain how you can tell.
questions.ms: Section C (1): the line is steeper / speed in A is 40 ÷ 4 = 10 m/s and in C is 15 m/s (1).

questions.q: Explain why atmospheric pressure is lower at the top of a mountain than at sea level.
questions.ms: There is less air (a smaller column of air) above you, so less weight of air pushing down (1); air is less dense / fewer particles in each cm³ (1); so fewer collisions of particles with a surface each second (1).

questions.q: A sealed can of gas is heated. Explain, in terms of particles, why the pressure inside the can increases.
questions.ms: Particles gain (kinetic) energy (1); they move faster (1); they hit the walls of the can more often (1) and with more force (1), so pressure increases.

questions.q:
A box has a weight of 600 N. Its base measures 0.5 m by 0.4 m.
Calculate the pressure the box exerts on the floor. Give the unit.
questions.ms: 3000 Pa (N/m²). M1 area = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2 m², M1 pressure = force ÷ area = 600 ÷ 0.2, A1 3000 Pa.

questions.q: Explain why people wear snowshoes to walk on soft snow. Use the equation for pressure in your answer.
questions.ms: Pressure = force ÷ area (1); snowshoes increase the area in contact with the snow (1); weight is the same, so the pressure is lower and they sink less (1).

questions.q: A dam holds back the water of a lake. The wall is much thicker at the bottom than at the top. Explain why.
questions.ms: Pressure in a liquid increases with depth (1) because there is more water (more weight) above pushing down (1); so the force on the bottom of the wall is greatest and it must be stronger/thicker there (1).

questions.q:
A force of 20 N is used on a spanner, 0.3 m from the nut.
Calculate the moment of the force.
questions.ms: 6 Nm. M1 moment = force × perpendicular distance from pivot = 20 × 0.3, A1 6 Nm.

questions.q:
A see-saw is balanced. A child weighing 300 N sits 2 m from the pivot. Another child sits 1.5 m from the pivot on the other side.
Calculate the weight of the second child.
questions.ms: 400 N. M1 clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment, M1 300 × 2 = W × 1.5, A1 W = 600 ÷ 1.5 = 400 N.

questions.q: Compare how pressure acts in solids, liquids and gases. Use ideas about particles in your answer.
questions.ms: Level 3 (5-6): clear comparison of all three with particle explanations. Level 2 (3-4): two states explained or three described. Level 1 (1-2): simple points. Points: solids pass pressure in the direction of the force, particles fixed in place; pressure on a surface depends on force and area; liquids: particles close together so liquids cannot be compressed, pressure acts in all directions and increases with depth (hydraulics); gases: particles far apart and moving randomly, pressure caused by particles colliding with the walls, gases can be compressed, pressure increases with temperature or less volume.

questions.q: Elements in the same group of the periodic table have…
options: the same number of electron shells
the same state at room temperature
questions.ms: Similar chemical properties (same number of electrons in the outer shell).

questions.q:
The table shows the boiling points of some Group 0 elements.
ElementBoiling point (°C)
Helium−269
Neon−246
Argon−186
Krypton−153
Xenon?
Describe the trend in boiling point and predict the boiling point of xenon.
questions.ms: Boiling point increases going down the group (1). Prediction between −140 and −90 °C (1) (actual −108 °C), with the reason that it continues the pattern / bigger atoms (1).

questions.q:
A student times a trolley rolling down a ramp from the same height four times.
RepeatTime (s)
12.4
22.6
33.9
42.5
Which result is anomalous?
questions.ms: 3.9 s, because it is much bigger than the others.

questions.q: Calculate the mean time, ignoring the anomalous result.
The student repeats the test at different ramp heights. As the height goes up, the time goes down. Describe the relationship and name the type of graph she should draw.
questions.ms: Negative relationship / as height increases, time decreases (1). Line graph or scatter graph, because both variables are continuous (1).

questions.q: Give one variable the student should keep the same, and explain why.
questions.ms: Any one control (1): same trolley/mass, same ramp surface, same length of ramp, same starting position, same person timing. Reason (1): so it is a fair test / only the height affects the time.
